summary: `dp[i][j]` stores the side of the biggest all-1 square whose bottom-right corner is (i, j). It equals 1 + the smallest of the three neighbours above, left and above-left (T13 — DP on a grid). The answer is the biggest value in the table.

blocks.title: Read the size
blocks.text: Rows and columns on one line: `split()` + `map(int, …)`.

blocks.title: Print the header and read the matrix
blocks.text: The program prints `Enter the matrix:` itself, then reads N lines without a prompt. Each line holds space-separated 0/1 values, so we split it and convert to `int`.

blocks.title: Set up the DP table
blocks.text: `dp` starts all zeros — a 0 cell can't be the corner of any square. `best = 0` matters: an all-zero matrix must print 0, not 1.

blocks.title: Visit every 1-cell, top to bottom
blocks.text: Going row by row, left to right, guarantees the top, left and top-left neighbours are already filled when we reach (i, j).

blocks.title: First row or first column
blocks.text: A cell on the top edge or left edge has no room for anything bigger than 1. Without this case, `dp[i - 1]` with i = 0 would silently read the LAST row.

blocks.title: Grow from the three neighbours
blocks.text: A k×k square ending here needs (k−1)-squares ending above, to the left and diagonally. The smallest of the three limits how far we can grow.

blocks.title: Track the largest square
blocks.text: Update `best` as we go, so we don't need a second pass over the table.

complexity: Time O(N·M); with 500×500 that is 250,000 cells (~0.15 s). Checking every square directly would be around 10¹⁰ steps.
pitfalls: Reading rows as strings when they are space-separated numbers.
Missing the first-row/first-column case → `dp[-1]` wraps around.
